A day later it had recovered almost all of the loss. Alerts like this one appear daily, and markets can react to them quickly. A few simple checks show how much an alert actually tells you. Understand what trackers can see, and what they can't Every transfer on a public blockchain such as Ethereum is visible: which address sent coins, which address received them, how many, and when. Analytics platforms such as Arkham Intelligence and services such as Lookonchain turn that data into readable alerts. Trackers can't see who owns an address unless it has been identified, and they can't see what happens inside an exchange. Once coins reach an exchange deposit address, any sale happens on the exchange's internal order book, which is not recorded on the blockchain. title: How Singapore's monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers
body: How Singapore's monetary policy works: the S$NEER band explained in three levers Most central banks fight inflation by raising or cutting interest rates. Singapore does it differently. The Monetary Authority of Singapore steers the economy by managing the value of the Singapore dollar against a basket of its trading partners' currencies. When MAS "tightens," it lets the currency strengthen faster, which makes imports cheaper and cools inflation. When it "eases," it slows or reverses that appreciation. That is why Wednesday's decision to hold policy steady was framed entirely in terms of an exchange rate band, with no mention of an interest rate. Why Singapore uses the exchange rate Singapore is one of the most open economies in the world. It imports most of what it consumes, from food and fuel to raw materials, and trade flows are large relative to the size of its economy. That makes the exchange rate a far more powerful influence on prices than domestic interest rates. There is also a practical constraint. Singapore allows capital to move freely in and out of the country. A central bank with open capital flows can control either its exchange rate or its interest rates, but not both. MAS chose the exchange rate in 1981, and local interest rates largely follow global rates, particularly those in the US. What is the S$NEER?

Goldman Sachs says yuan undervalued by up to 25% and markets underestimate how far it can rise China operates a managed floating exchange rate system, under which the renminbi (yuan) is allowed to trade within a prescribed band around a central reference rate, or midpoint, set each trading day by the PBOC. The current trading band permits the currency to move plus or minus 2% from the official midpoint during onshore trading hours. Each morning, the PBOC determines the midpoint based on a range of inputs. These include the previous day's closing price, movements in major currencies, particularly the US dollar, broader international FX conditions, and domestic economic considerations such as capital flows, growth momentum and financial stability objectives. The midpoint is not a purely mechanical calculation, allowing policymakers discretion to guide market expectations. Once the midpoint is announced, onshore USD/CNY is free to trade within the allowable band. If market pressures push the yuan toward either edge of that range, the central bank may step in to smooth volatility.

This was the highest rate since June, driven primarily by faster non-food inflation (1.5% vs 1.2% in August). The main contributor was a sharper rise in transport costs (4.3% vs 2.5%), reflecting higher fuel prices and stronger travel demand ahead of the Golden Week holidays. Additional upward pressure came from clothing (1.2% vs 1.3%), healthcare (2.7% vs 2.7%), and education (1.4% vs 1.4%). By contrast, housing costs remained weak, registering a decline of 0.3% for the second consecutive month (-0.3% vs -0.3%). Food prices fell for the sixth consecutive month (-1.7% vs -1.4%), led by a further drop in pork prices, as abundant supply and subdued consumption continued to drag on the market. On a monthly basis, consumer prices increased 0.2%, undershooting forecasts of a 0.3% rise and easing from August's 0.4% gain, which had been the strongest monthly increase since February. title: China's Consumer Inflation Cools in September, Signaling Softer Price Momentum
body: China's consumer price growth eased in September 2026, with the Consumer Price Index (CPI) rising 0.2% month-over-month, down from a 0.4% increase in August. The latest data, updated on 14 October 2026, indicate a loss of short-term price momentum in the world's second-largest economy. The month-over-month reading shows that prices in September grew at only half the pace seen in August. In the comparison framework used, the "actual" figure reflects the change from August to September, while the "previous" figure captures the change from July to August. The slowdown from 0.4% to 0.2% will likely be watched closely by markets assessing the strength and breadth of China's domestic demand. title: China's Producer Prices Accelerate in September, Signaling Stronger Industrial Momentum
body: China's Producer Price Index (PPI) accelerated in September 2026, rising 5.0% year-over-year, up from 3.8% in August, according to data updated on 14 October 2026. The figures highlight a notable strengthening in price pressures at the factory gate, as the pace of producer inflation quickened by 1.2 percentage points in just one month. The PPI measures the average change over time in the selling prices received by domestic producers for their output, and this data is reported on a year-over-year basis. The "previous" reading of 3.8% for August 2026 reflected price changes compared with August a year earlier, while the current 5.0% September reading compares prices to September of the prior year. The acceleration suggests rising costs in China's industrial sector, with potential implications for corporate margins and, if passed on, for consumer inflation both domestically and abroad.
